description: This female which I mistook for another kind of merganser instead of a Hooded Merganser was sitting on the bank of the park with a bunch of other ducks. I have seen the females once before earlier last year but at a great distance using only the Camera to help my vision. I have never seen one this close before. She was very beautiful but had the most weirdest feathers on her head. Most mergansers have what I call the hairdo. They are very elaborate with their head feathers. The Hooded Merganser especially; they look like fire place billows when they raise their crests to show if they are alarmed or to show off for mates and keeping rival males at bay. Hooded Mergansers are a very unique bird and are one of the most interesting characters in the bird world. They are one of my favorites. The males are more colorful than the females but they seem to still chose the browns, blacks, and whites as their colors while the female is brown with some white. They are small and like most diving ducks they sit low in the water when they swim. This is the first time I have seen a Merganser on land. It was one interesting encounter.

She Looks Different
I kept losing sight of her as larger ducks would block the way.  When I finally got a clear shot, she looked different.  Her crest was down which gave her a sleek appearance.  I could also see her long tail this time.  Unfortunately she spotted me and slipped into the water behind her and disappeared.  Back to being elusive.

description: I had begun to positively love being an outdoorsman. Dad said that somehow, by the grace of God or men (depending on religious inclination), I had lucked into managing the best fishery in the Northeast corner of Southwest Miami County. And none of the adults seemed to care how I was managing it. Not even the scientists. Lately there had been one that had stopped in to see Dad, a scientist I mean. The men in the neighborhood were still trying to perfect the size of the bass in the big lake. One man, a hunter, was really into ducks. My understanding is that Jerry spent time with his brother restoring a wetland in the far western reaches of Miami County. He had an old green jon-boat stored in his garage that had a duck blind built around it. The shape of it was sort of like a tank with high plywood side walls painted green. There were slits cut in the side walls of the plywood so the men, sitting in the boat, could peek out at the ducks without being seen. When one stood to fire, you could only see him from the shoulders up. The rest of him still hidden from the ducks behind the side walls of the boat. It was even outfitted with its own Ghillie suit. Basically, a hula skirt ringing the entire green-painted plywood side walls of the jon-boat. One time Ole’ Jerry showed me a small, funny looking horn he and his brother would blow to attract the ducks. I liked to imagine these men hunkering down in their boat, taking turns blowing the little horn. When the ducks would come, it’s hard to know what attracted the ducks to the men. Was it the funny little horn, the restored wetland, or God? Dad would have answered, “yes”. On this particular occasion, Dad asked the scientist about Jerry. Jerry had been building these contraptions to place around the lake. The contraptions were what I now know are called nest boxes. They were made of plywood and painted green. They were taller than they were wide and they had a good sized hole cut out of the top. Jerry and his brother were sinking them on posts here and there along the far side of the bank of the big lake. The near side of the big lake was residential lawns (some with very mature trees) running down hill and right up to the water's edge. Ole’ Jerry had the enormous good fortune of owning one of these houses that sat on the hill overlooking the lake. He left binoculars on his table behind the window so he could peek out, at any moment. You know, to see how the ducks were doing. It seemed funny to me, that a man who spent so much time hiding from ducks and peeking out at them, would also spend time building boxes for the ducks to hide in and peek out at him. I asked Ole’ Jerry about this one time. He said that long, long back most of Ohio was forest. Back then, the farmer’s field that began just after the far bank of the big lake wouldn’t have existed. It would have been forest. There would have been plenty of cavities in dead trees for his ducks to nest in and peek out at him. If Ole’ Jerry had just needed something to eat, he could have easily bought it at the meat market. It seems silly to have to restore an entire wetland, build an elaborate boat, and build a bunch of nest boxes just to have some duck meat. But like I say, Ole’ Jerry loved those ducks. I have never since met a man that loved ducks more than he did. I was up at the big lake on November 25th, 2015 and noticed these endangered mergansers. I imagined Ole’ Jerry tooting his small funny looking horn and peeking down on them. I was there to observe the far side of the lake before Dad and Ole’ Jerry caught hold of it (3rd pic - 1973). And I was there in 2015 bearing witness to the result (1st two pics). But which phrase to choose, “observation” or “bearing witness”. Dad would have said “yes, but if you want to know which one specifically, ask a scientist or a duck hunter”.

description:
This one is for the mergansers
Photo 1:
Mom's Life Lessons
Mama was teaching her chicks how to catch crawdads.  She dove 7 came back up with a big one.
Photo 2:
Mom Does Not Share
One chick looks for its own food and the other chick looks like it wants mom's crawdad.  Hooded mergansers do not feed their babies.  They do lead them to good food spots and demonstrate how to do it.  Most babies live on insects until they can figure out how to dive and catch fish and other aquatic critters.  These babies are lucky because their mom has led them to a place with lots of food so they learn how to eat well early in life.  I saw the babies having lots of success in catching their own crawdads.  Most of that behavior took place where there was too much shrubbery or it was too dark for me to get shots. Junior Dropped His Crawfish

description:
With Don Fraser; my first visit here ... this year (?)! We skipped a walk-around survey and immediately settled into a Gulfwatch from the southern gazebo. The weather at the start was overcast, light sprinkling (which ended quickly), 64 degrees ("feels like" 64), with a light breeze. Once we found the Red-throated Loon, the survey sort of ended, as we were watching the loon while friends were en route to see it. Christine Rowland and Vince Capp arrived in time to see the loon, but Dave Bowman arrived a few minutes too late; the loon got up and flew north -- toward Hudson Marina -- after maybe 35 minutes. 

The Red-throated Loon was a NEW photographed bird for me for Florida!  And, it is the first photographically documented record for Pasco County! (Hudson Beach comes through again!).

The Helmeted Guineafowl was QUITE the surprise: according to Vince, it is imprinted on the Mallards and even follows them into the water!

Speaking of Mallards, we saw at least 42, with many aberrant plumages that I guess are the result of inbreeding.

We left at 0938 and headed to SunWest Park.

"Small diving duck with thin serrated bill. Breeding males have showy black-and-white crest, a couple zebra stripes on the white breast, and cinnamon-colored sides. Females are brown with a puffy crest and partly yellow bill. Looks slender and long-necked in flight, with very fast wingbeats. Widespread across much of North America, but usually only seen in pairs or small flocks. Nests in cavities near small ponds or marshes; especially fond of wooded swamps. description: With Valeri Ponzo; successful year-birding (we each got the same three species). The weather was sunny, clear, and cold (38 degrees but "feels like" 44), with a light breeze. We owe a debt of thanks to Kim Leedom for posting her checklist for Dike 131 on 22 Dec 2020. We followed Kim's lead to great advantage, parking at the junction of the main refuge road and Dike 132, then walking south along Dike 132 to Dike 131, then east to the duck flocks; we returned to Jet by back-tracking the entire walk. The night before, while planning our itinerary for the refuge, I realized that we'd be looking right into the rising sun if we walked the dike first thing in the morning. So we waited 2.5 hours -- and still were looking largely into the sun. But eventually the dike angled northeast and we got good light on the third pile of birds (the first two piles mostly were silhouettes). We were pressed for time -- we had to leave by 1330 for me to be home by 2200 -- so we made rough estimate of the duck numbers and scanned for rarities. No doubt we overlooked several species due to limited time, distance to some of the flocks, and at times poor lighting; we honestly could have spent several hours along this trail. We left at 1144 and birded two more areas of the refuge before heading home at 1347.

Two Hooded Mergansers (Lophodytes cucullatus) can be seen here. Spotted in moraine state park at 3:30 on 12/4/2024. Though the pictures are hard to tell I was able to identify the mergansers with binoculars. The mergansers were identifiable by there small size, thin bills, the crest of there head, the dark black and brown body, and the black head with white starting behind the eye going into the crest. The mergansers habitat is most forested wetland but with the bays and marsh areas being frozen, they can be seen here moving into open water of the lake. They will winter in Pennsylvania if there is open water and are native to this area. They birds were seen below a flock of ring billed gulls (larus delwarenis). Both the mergansers and the gulls were seen diving in the water after a school of what I believe were alewife (alosa pseudoharengus). The majority of the mergansers diet is fish in this case alewife are the most predominant baitfish in Lake Arthur. The weather during the sighting was cloudy and 31f with a high of 34f and a low of 20f. The wind was 13mph SW with 1.6 inches of snow that day, humidity was at 73%.

Hooded Merganser - Lophodytes cucullatus (male, female)
iNaturalist says "Conservation Status: critically imperiled (S1B,S4N) in North Carolina, US (NatureServe)". 
That might be true for breeding birds recently, but it is a common species in winter.
I think the NatureServe status needs updates as well, as it has been found breeding recently at a number of sites--even in the lower Piedmont of the Triangle area. This is a bit of good news for the species.
